  • The coming years will bring with them the Prime Video TV show Fourth Wing, based on Rebecca Yarros' bestselling The Empyrean romantasy book series.
  • Sources indicate that amazon MGM Studios officially ordered the Fourth Wing series in May 2026, so the project is still in the early stages of development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, michael B. Jordan has an absolutely massive fantasy project on the way with Prime Video. It seems that, in recent years, this genre has completely overtaken the entertainment industry, but that only makes it that much harder to make an impact. The success of Game of Thrones inspired a massive wave of projects, some of which succeeded while many more have failed. With this oversaturation, it's difficult to predict what will land with viewers, and there's no longer a guarantee that TV highlights based on popular fantasy book series will succeed. Still, there are exceptions.

The coming years will bring with them the Prime Video TV show Fourth Wing, based on Rebecca Yarros' bestselling The Empyrean romantasy book series. When looking at the premise of these novels, it's easy to see how they became such hits. The story revolves around the protagonist, Violet Sorrengail, as she navigates a fantasy world that demands brutal effort to become a dragon rider. It's success or death, and this dynamic is further intensified by Fourth Wing's open-door, steamy romance.

Sources indicate that amazon MGM Studios officially ordered the Fourth Wing series in May 2026, so the project is still in the early stages of development. Still, we already know that there are some truly excellent names attached. Michael B. Jordan is executive producing through his organization, Outlier Society, while Meredith Averill (The Haunting of Hill House) will serve as showrunner. Yarros herself is closely involved with the Fourth Wing TV show, as she will executive-produce alongside Athena Wickham, Elizabeth Raposo, and Sherryl Clark.

Recent findings suggest that as further evidence that Prime Video is taking its Fourth Wing TV series extremely seriously, the first small round of casting has already been completed. Jordan previously stated that he wanted relative newcomers to star in the series, thus avoiding cheesy pandering that might break the immersion. Prime followed through with the news that Esther McGregor will play Violet Sorrengail while Emilio Sakraya takes on the role of Xaden Riorson. Suffice it to say, Fourth Wing is gaining easy momentum, so it's clear this project is expected to be a pretty major deal.

There have been several hopeful fantasy projects to hit the scene in the 2020s, many of which were expected to be as major a deal as Game of Thrones. Prime Video's The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is the most expensive fantasy TV show ever made—a significant indicator that MGM planned for it to be its flagship fantasy after previous failures. While Rings of Power has done well in its own way, it by no means struck the scene as the same sort of fantasy event as Game of Thrones. This comes down to a primary struggle that Fourth Wing shouldn't face.

It has been revealed that when it comes down to it, Rings of Power requires a lot from its viewers. This is a prequel in a larger franchise, which means audiences must have some foundational knowledge of Lord of the Rings. This makes it a niche project regardless of the budget. The same is true for other fantasy TV shows of the decade. HBO expanded Game of Thrones into House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, neither of which has been quite as substantial as their parent series. Even fantasy projects like The Witcher, which picks up midway within the lore, ask too much of mainstream viewers.

Industry observers note that fourth Wing is uniquely equipped to avoid this problem while delivering on all the key high points of the fantasy genre. As a dragon rider story full of adult themes, this show will check off some of the same boxes as Game of Thrones. As a brand-fresh TV show that picks up right at the beginning of a fairly recently established fantasy adventure, Fourth Wing will be highly accessible to any adult viewer who happens to tune in. This is, essentially, the birth of something new—a chance to experience the fantasy event of the decade from day one.

The NCIS franchise has been around for well over 20 years, and while it may have begun with just one, it has turned into a web of the most talented operatives around the world working together to stop crime. One creator who has been involved with the franchise for years now is R. Scott Gemmill, who first worked with LL COOL J and Chris O’Donnell on the hit series, NCIS: Los Angeles. He reunited with LL COOL J all these years later for the new NCIS series, NCIS: New York. If Gemmill's name sounds familiar, it's because he's also the creator of The Pitt, the fan-favorite hospital show on HBO Max starring Noah Wyle.

According to recent reports, new episodes of both the original NCIS series and the aforementioned LL COOL J-led spin-off, NCIS: New York, can be seen on CBS every week. As for the prequel show, NCIS: Origins, new installments also drop every Tuesday, and all three shows are set to come to a head next year. Each series is going on a mid-season break soon, but, CBS still has plenty to give NCIS viewers in the next few months. Last week, Paramount announced a handful of new release dates for its mid-season primetime schedule for the 2026-2027 network TV season. This confirmed that the fan-favorite spin-off NCIS: Sydney, will premiere its fourth season on Tuesday, January 26 at 10 pm, with NCIS: New York airing a special original episode after the AFC Championship game on CBS on Sunday, January 31. NCIS, NCIS: Origins, and NCIS: New York will also return from their mid-season breaks on Tuesday, January 12, with NCIS: Origins airing its Season 3 finale one week later, on Tuesday, January 19.

Recent findings suggest that NCIS fans who are looking for another series to scratch the signature crime thriller itch should look no further than Tracker, which stars Justin Hartley and Jensen Ackles. Lost veteran Josh Holloway also recently debuted in the latest episode of Tracker, which already has fans asking more questions about potential spin-offs. More watchable CBS indicates include Cupertino, the newly introduced legal thriller starring Mike Colter from Marvel's Luke Cage franchise, Matlock, the legal drama starring Kathy Bates, as well as other series such as Ghosts, Einstein, and even Survivor.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps.
  • Sources indicate that the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027.
  • It has been revealed that “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what owners need to know.

Sources indicate that the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

It has been revealed that “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”.

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly notes it has no prepares for a native Mac app.

In a recent development, you can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft intends to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the firm.

Recent findings suggest that the June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Upgrade: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:.

“We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team looks. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iPadOS 27.3 is now in beta and will launch to all customers next month, here are three newly introduced features it introduces for iPad.

According to recent reports, there’s a new setting in iPadOS 27.3 that I instantly turned on and have been loving. It lets you double-tap the top of a window to resize it.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if ‘Windowed Apps’ is enabled there’s now a new toggle: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom.’.

I’ve been using this gesture all the time in the beta, because it lets me resize my window to fullscreen then revert it to its previous size with ease. It’s an intuitive, convenient way to resize windows for different tasks.

Read more: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on.

Visual intelligence was available on iPad already, but iPadOS 27.3 adds a dedicated hub for using the feature: a new Siri mode in the Camera app.

iOS 27 brought Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app, but it was missing from iPad. iPadOS 27.3 corrects that oversight, letting you use your iPad’s built-in Camera app to ask Siri about any object you capture.

Baking visual intelligence into Camera should expose the feature to a lot more iPad users, since before you had to set up a custom control or shortcut for it. And with how much better visual intelligence has gotten thanks to Siri AI, the Siri mode is a valuable addition.

Read more: iOS 27 gives the Camera app on iPhone a brand upcoming mode.

Freeform is gaining a variety of new features in iPadOS 27.3. They’re available in macOS and iOS too, but out of all Apple platforms, Freeform feels very much built for the iPad.

Which iPadOS 27.3 features are you most looking forward to? Let us know in the comments.

Editor's note: The below contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4 Episode 4.

The Gilded Age Season 4 has already delivered more than a few surprises, ranging from the identity of George's (Morgan Spector) shooter to Jack's (Ben Ahlers) latest romance. There are plenty of storylines to watch, but with the season hitting its halfway point, one reveal about Marian (Louisa Jacobson) changes everything for her future. Throughout the series, Marian's romance with Larry (Harry Richardson) has had its ups and downs; even once they got engaged in Season 3, things didn't go smoothly, with the two ultimately deciding to call things off despite lingering feelings.

Recent findings suggest that season 4's latest episode makes Marian and Larry's romance more complicated than ever when Marian realizes she could be pregnant with Larry's child. Following their night together in the season premiere, fans speculated about the possibility of a pregnancy occurring, but the confirmation is still a shock that will impact their potential future. Given the time period, this twist is especially significant, and it will permanently alter Marian's life, however she chooses to proceed. With The Gilded Age now renewed for Season 5, it's safe to say fans will get to see the fallout — however it plays out for the remainder of Season 4 and beyond.

Sources indicate that the Gilded Age's latest reveal comes at the end of Episode 4 when, after a few nosebleeds, Marian's friend at the Settlement House, Virginia Saville (Elizabeth Marvel), suggests it could be related to menstruation, prompting Marian to realize how long it's been since she had her last period. This pregnancy is shocking for many reasons, first and foremost being the potential danger to her reputation. After her near-elopement with Mr. Raikes (Thomas Cocquerel) in Season 1, Marian has taken care to protect what standing she has in society. Her caution partly contributed to her breakup with Larry last season, but this new turn of events will be even more challenging to keep under wraps.

According to recent reports, the Gilded Age has touched on similar scandals before, most notably with Mrs. Chamberlain (Jeanne Tripplehorn), who remains an outcast in society decades later. Though the two cases aren't the same, this storyline illustrates how Marian may be treated if or when the truth comes out. Her aunt Agnes (Christine Baranski) will undoubtedly disapprove, putting Marian in a difficult spot at home. Although Agnes continues to evolve in her views, she has previously shown a willingness to distance herself from scandal, most recently including her initial reaction to Aurora Fane's (Kelli O'Hara) divorce. Unless she can hide this pregnancy, Marian is headed for social ruin and ostracization — but there may be a way to salvage the situation.

In a recent development, while Season 4's storyline is a major twist for Marian, it could end the will-they-won't-they between her and Larry, which would be welcome, while also helping her conceal that she became pregnant beforehand. #142760. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2884 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to significant issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • According to recent reports, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to significant issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

According to recent reports, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he indicates he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

It has been revealed that ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to substantial issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

According to recent reports, andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having mentioned that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a fresh paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having stated that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and stated, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing newly introduced here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Industry observers note that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and noted, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

In a recent development, the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that demonstrated up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from massive data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Recent findings suggest that ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having mentioned that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Industry observers note that could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Sources indicate that ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Fresh tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an notable piece of the puzzle.

Industry observers note that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention rapidly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

According to recent reports, for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

According to recent reports, ng: I think synthetic data is an key tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

According to recent reports, ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion people. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Sources indicate that synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a tech giant approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

According to recent reports, ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

In a recent development, one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

Sources indicate that how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift problem. I find it really crucial to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and enhancement the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In a recent development, in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s vital for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

According to recent reports, ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rian Johnson successfully brought the star-studded murder mystery back to the significant screen with Knives Out, which has continued on with two Netflix sequels. He also turned to the small screen for a similar project that earned rave reviews for its two seasons, but now, unfortunately, the mystery is gone. Johnson recently revealed that, despite an attempt to revive it in a very unconventional fashion, the series has taken on its last case.

Poker Face debuted in 2023 on Peacock. The series starred Natasha Lyonne as Charle Cale, a woman with the uncanny talent to detect lies. Pursued by criminals after solving a murder, she took to the road in her 1969 Plymouth Barracuda; invariably, wherever she found herself, she'd be called upon to use her skills to sniff out a criminal. The series was cancelled by Peacock after its second season, but Johnson pitched the series to other outlets with a twist: Lyonne would be replaced by Peter Dinklage, who would be playing the same character.

Unfortunately, now we'll never find out how Johnson would have pulled off that strange metamorphosis. In a newly introduced interview with Variety, Johnson revealed that the series is dead and buried. Johnson ultimately wasn't able to make the re-cast make sense: "I got very excited about the notion of going out there with Dinklage, but then the more we kind of explored it, the more it kind of didn’t really make sense." However, he is hoping to collaborate with the Wicker star in the future: "...hopefully I can do something else with him someday. He’s the best." Johnson is staying busy: he's producing Joseph Gordon-Levitt's new thriller 2034, and is gearing up to begin production on a new science fiction conspiracy thriller of his own next year.

In the second season of Poker Face, Cale crosses paths with a mysterious assassin known only as the Iguana, even as she found a upcoming friend in the form of Alex (Patti Harrison, I Think You Should Leave). However, after stumbling upon the Iguana's latest victims, Charlie realizes Alex is the Iguana; bored by her life as an assassin, Alex had trailed herself to fool Charlie's senses. The two of them end up in the Barracuda as it speeds towards a cliff. Charlie escapes, but Alex seemingly perishes as it crashes to the ground. Charlie, now wanted by the FBI as the Iguana's accomplice, hitchhikes away with a trucker as the wrecked Barracuda is recovered with no sign of Alex's body.

In a recent development, both seasons of Poker Face are now streaming on Peacock. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#142755. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1282 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you know “the look” by now.
  • In a recent development, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

In a recent development, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

Sources indicate that the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT revealed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

Industry observers note that the generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

It has been revealed that this is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

Industry observers note that to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Recent findings suggest that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of latest features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a newly introduced setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

Industry observers note that you can also move the upcoming slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

According to recent reports, do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

Sources indicate that you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Industry observers note that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In a recent development, in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Sources indicate that here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

In a recent development, okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

It has been revealed that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Recent findings suggest that nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that halfway through her live-to-acetate set at Jack White’s Third Man Records in Nashville on Nov. 22, Olivia Rodrigo had a confession to make.

“Anybody that knows me at all knows that I’m kind of the biggest Jack White fan ever,” Rodrigo told the crowd at the intimate venue, gathered to watch her perform a tight set of songs at the label’s venue, the Blue Room, recorded for Third Man Records. “I was contemplating whether or not I’d say this, but given that we’re settling in, I thought I would come clean and admit that when I was 15, I did have a Jack White fan account called Third Fan Records. It’s kind of embarrassing in concept, but all this is to say that I think 15-year-old Olivia would be pretty stoked if you told her what she was doing tonight.”.

White took the stage to introduce Rodrigo himself before she played two 20-minute sets with a quick break in the middle to flip the record – guests in attendance could watch the whole process live on a screen that broadcasts into the venue during the show. “We’re going to have an outstanding artist come on stage here in a second,” White noted, before welcoming Rodrigo and her band who opened with “Ballad of a Homeschooled Girl” from Guts and played songs like the Grammy-nominated “The Cure,” “Stupid Song,” “Maggots For Brains,” “Déjà vu,” “All-American Bitch” and “Bad Idea Right?” Trending Stories Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Marry at Palm Springs Wedding Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Princess of Wales Reflects on Cancer Battle in ‘Heal’ Documentary Special Watch Olivia Rodrigo Cover ‘Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground’ at Jack White’s Blue Room.

And true to her commitment to White (telling the audience that the White Stripes is “my favorite band ever,” to the point she almost wore one of Meg White’s dresses to her inaugural Daisy Chain Festival) Rodrigo also performed a dynamite cover of the duo’s “Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground” from White Blood Cells. In a plaid skirt and shirt with “Upcoming York Confuses Me” printed across the front (which is yet another White Stripes nod), Rodrigo seemed completely at home at the tiny 250-capacity venue that’s just a touch smaller than the 20,000 or so seats she fills at arenas, the consummate rock star at both. Watching as the blue “cutting” light illuminated to signal the process was rolling and presided over by Third Man Team Members in lab coats, it all felt like a temporary, perfectly analog refuge from the looming AI hellscape waiting outside.

Industry observers note that everyone from Billie Eilish to Pearl Jam and Geese have recorded live-to-acetate at Third Man Records, with zero overdubs, pauses, or edits. The albums are eventually available for purchase after the pressing process is complete, sometimes earlier for members of Third Man’s Vault.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling fresh approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ever since appearing in the original Clerks in 1994, Jay and Silent Bob have become pop culture icons, popping up well beyond Kevin Smith's View Askewniverse. From an appearance in last year's wine comedy Napa Boys to a cameo in a Dunkin' commercial with Ben and Casey Affleck, showing up on the set of the latest Stab movie in Scream 3, and appearing in Archie comics, they continue to find themselves in strange new places three decades later, and they have a third solo movie on the way. So recognizable are the pair that they've become practically synonymous with Smith and Jason Mewes themselves whenever they appear on-screen. However, for once, the duo are playing roles together that aren't their instantly recognizable stoners or a nod to stated pair.

Sources indicate that this Wednesday, November 25, Smith and Mewes will be heading to Disney+ to join the world of young Cricket Green. Big City Greens Season 5, Episode 8, features two upcoming tales involving the titular family, starting with "Perked Up," which sees Doug Perkins regaling Gloria with his adventures alongside the Greens. However, the second half, "Chicken Coup," introduces the inseparable Jay and Silent Bob actors as a new dynamic duo — Ricky (Mewes) and Dave (Smith), two starving coyotes who encounter the Greens' power-hungry rooster, Cogburn (Alfred Molina), in the woods. Ahead of the episode's arrival on streaming, Collider can exclusively share a new sneak peek that sees them circling the fearsome fowl, but he may have a plan to avoid becoming chicken dinner.

According to recent reports, the footage opens with Cogburn's audience of forest creatures fleeing upon the arrival of Ricky and Dave, who look more fearsome than the average coyote. They each appear as if they've been in a scrap or two before, with the former missing part of his ear and the latter having an intimidating scar running down his left eye that matches Cogburn's. Like the predators, the Spider-Man villain-voiced rooster is no slouch in a fight, but his biggest asset is his brain and his charisma.

He catches them off guard by feigning sympathy for the coyotes' hunger, promising them an endless bounty of food from his farm if they follow him. To prove he's serious, he promises a way around the electric fence that keeps wreaking havoc on Ricky and Dave's hunt. With that, he has two new loyal soldiers for his army, which he'll presumably use to get revenge on the Greens and take what he desires.

Recent findings suggest that though they're not as raunchy as usual, Smith and Mewes still bring a bit of their chemistry and humor to Significant City Greens. They add to a lengthy Season 5 guest roster, headlined by the return of former The Suite Life of Zach & Cody star Dylan Sprouse to Disney. Stephen King, Luke Combs, Chad Michael Murray, Meghan Stalter, Cobie Smulders, Clark Gregg, Mike Colter, and Steve Scirripa are also among the big names appearing in this latest run. Speaking to Collider's Maggie Lovitt, Mewes was thrilled to join the adventures of the mischievous Cricket and his family in part because his kids loved the show. It was also a rare opportunity for him and Smith to do something outside their typical wheelhouse together that still played to their friendship.

"It was great because, again, it was — we're not, I know, as people who know Kevin well and myself, we're not very scary, so it was cool to be sort of a scary character in there and get to play sort of scary. All the other animals were like, 'Whoa,' but then, being part of it, and then all of a sudden, there's this twist at the end. But again, it was fun because coyotes. I mean, any animal would be great, but to get to play a coyote was fantastic. And, you know, they roll in packs, so again, Kevin and I together as a pack, beautiful.".

It has been revealed that major City Greens Season 5, Episode 8 arrives on Disney+ on November 25. Check out our exclusive sneak peek in the player above and stay tuned at Collider for more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a personal trainer, I blueprint my sessions the same way every time: a mobility-focused warm-up, the session plan itself, then a cool-down full of deep holds and static stretches.

The idea is to prepare your joints and muscles for movement and encourage blood flow around the body, which you won't really do by folding over your legs to stretch your hamstrings.

Building flexible muscles and mobile joints isn't just about sitting cross-legged or touching your toes; it's about combining strength, balance, control and stability, and increasing range of motion.

Industry observers note that the next time you warm up before a run, try these three dynamic exercises instead. Below, I show you how to do them and why.

It has been revealed that if you experience pain at any time, stop and rest. If you're working with an injury or health condition, or you're currently pregnant or postnatal, I recommend seeking advice before starting these exercises.

The routine: 50 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 3 rounds. Add or reduce the number of rounds if you prefer.

If you run often or you watch a lot of soccer, you know how nasty a hamstring injury can be, and how long it takes to recover. It can come out of nowhere, too, sending you into a slow, painful hobble. We want to avoid that by warming these tender muscle groups properly before a workout, and to do that, I encourage you to add gentle motion to your warm-ups.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Recent findings suggest that really, these three moves target more than just your hamstrings, but I highly recommend them as part of a wider routine or as a standalone session. If you have very tight muscles, a soft knee bend will help in downward dog, and during the Cossack squat, reducing your squat depth will be helpful.

It has been revealed that keeping active and moving around often will also move blood around the body, delivering more oxygen to the working muscle groups. Equally, staying on your feet longer means activating your calves, which are known as the second heart, as contracting the calf muscles pumps deoxygenated blood back toward the heart.

The moral of the story? Walk (and practice mobility) before you run.

I t was subzero in Grafton, North Dakota, when Liz O’Toole’s water broke. She roused her husband, Terry Morrison, his brown mullet tousled on the pillow beside her, and grabbed her hospital bag, plus a towel to keep the truck seat dry on the 43-minute trip to Unity Medical Center, a low-slung building where generations of Morrison’s family had been born.

But after nurses wheeled her into the facility, things took a turn. She was told her pelvic bones were too small and that she’d need to have a C-section.

Morrison watched through the window, his stomach too weak to take in the blood. A few hours later,  when the baby was finally clean and swaddled, he held his son for the first time. The nurses helped O’Toole breastfeed and rolled black ink on her baby’s feet, stamping them at the bottom of the birth certificate. They named their one and only child Jeremy; Terry liked the name. Simple as that.

In a recent development, later that evening, Evelyn Newton finally let her husband, Keith Bylin, drive her to Unity Medical Center after labor had well and truly set in. This was her second child, and she knew that if she got to the hospital too soon, they’d confine her to a bed for hours on end. She’s not one to sit idle, even with a baby on the way. Bylin watched the ice crystals in the sky float under the moon, his fair cheeks ruddy with the cold, as they motored the 30 miles to the delivery room. The puce-green tiles looked dated to him, the room stark and bare. Same as the other couple, after giving birth, the nurses helped Newton nurse and stamped the baby’s feet at the bottom of the birth certificate, which read “Kyle Jerome Bylin.”.

In a recent development, the babies went home a few days later: Jeremy to a single-wide trailer, where he dozed in a borrowed bassinet next to his parents’ bed; Kyle to the Bylin family farm and a hand-cranked baby swing in his older brother Darren’s room. Both were sweet babies, good sleepers. Kyle loved to be tickled until he squirmed — then tickled again. Jeremy begged his mom for baths. Both were loved. In a recent development, aside from being white men born on the same day in the same hospital, Kyle and Jeremy don’t have too much in common these days. Kyle is a research librarian, enamored with technology. Jeremy works as a welding inspector for a wind-energy company and loves cars. Since that night back in 1988, they’ve lived 36 years without crossing paths. Still, they’re tied together by an unimaginable trauma. Somehow, they got mixed up back in the nursery, each going home wearing a hospital bracelet meant for the other child — and lived the life the other was supposed to live.

Industry observers note that now, after DNA revealed the shocking secret, the families are looking for answers. And demanding justice.

Industry observers note that KYLE BYLIN GREW UP IN THE FARMING town of Adams, North Dakota, population 121. Boasting barely more than a church, grocery, bank, and gas station, it’s the kind of place where family ties go back for centuries. The Bylin farm has been around for four generations; angus cows and Paso Fino horses graze in the football-size front yard, which abuts the glittering Bylin Dam.

Obsessed with technology and rock & roll, Kyle wasn’t too keen on exploring the thick woods behind his house or wrangling cattle. As a kid, he’d cry if his mother tried to coax him up on horseback. Instead, he’d steal himself away in his bedroom or the basement, writing his own Dashboard Confessional-inspired lyrics on message boards as his brother and his father worked on Darren’s prized 1989 Nissan 240SX in the garage. Out his window, Kyle could see the silver grain silos wavering in the summer heat, his family’s land stretching off toward the horizon. This was supposed to be his future: working with his hands the way Bylins had done for generations. Not an ideal path for a kid who regularly trekked to Grand Forks to see the likes of Ozzy Osbourne, Mudvayne, and Rob Zombie wreak havoc on the Alerus Center stage. Still, Kyle never suspected that his family wasn’t, well, his. In family photos, he doesn’t look markedly different: There’s a Christmas snapshot of him, his dad, and Darren where he’s sporting one of those metal-ball necklaces that were so popular in the Nineties and a Slipknot T-shirt, his dark Caesar cut and glasses making him look like a young Freddie Prinze Jr. His father and Darren are more clean-cut, rugged blond Norwegians with rosy cheeks, but they all have the same intense, sparkling eyes. And then there’s his mom, Evelyn, petite and fine-boned with caramel curls. They’re not exactly twins, but any differences Kyle may have noticed between him and his family could be explained by Evelyn’s background: She was adopted by an American soldier in Germany during the Cold War. Her father was a chief warrant officer, so she spent her childhood shuttling between bases, learning to walk on the boat over to Ellis Island.

Kyle’s parents got divorced when he was in grade school, so he doesn’t really have any memories of them together — just shuttling between the farm and his mom’s trailer. But his childhood memories are mostly happy ones: shooting down a waterslide that seemed as tall as a building at Disney World with his brother, watching Old Faithful erupt with his dad, showing his mom a newly introduced litter of kittens up in the hayloft, their eyes still closed and fur damp.

Recent findings suggest that while Darren followed in his father’s bootprints and joined the family farm, Kyle enrolled in a state university for a spell — the first in his clan to get a higher education. His path to a degree was circuitous though; he dropped out of that first school and became a music-tech journalist in Los Angeles, before following a girlfriend to Iowa, where she’d gotten a job.

Seated in a circle at his girlfriend’s parents’ house back home in Columbus, Ohio, fate intervened in 2017. Under the soft glow of Christmas lights, Kyle rifled through the pile of secret-Santa gifts in search of the most promising box. His girlfriend’s mom had gone all out: lotto tickets, candles, wine, you name it. When he pulled back the festive paper, though, Kyle glimpsed the distinctive, leaf-shaped logo of Ancestry.com, a prominent DNA-testing firm. “I took it home and sent off the test and didn’t really think anything of it for a long time,” he says. Until years later, when he’d receive a message that changed everything.

IF YOU FOLLOW NORTH DAKOTA’S RED RIVER about an hour south from Kyle’s childhood home, you’ll eventually run into the single-wide where Jeremy grew up with his mom after his parents split in grade school. Unlike Kyle, Jeremy spent most of his childhood outside: building forts with other kids in the trailer park, catching frogs and lizards in the woods, and working on his red 1990 Nissan 240 SX.

Sources indicate that his mother was happy for her son to be outdoors exploring while she was busy working. Liz O’Toole helped locals recover after the Red River flooded back in 1997, making sure everyone had the proper materials to rebuild. Later on, she got her master’s and worked at a rehab center. It was a childhood out of an adventure book, but Jeremy never felt quite right in his family. His parents were dark-haired and solid, while Jermey looked like Dennis the Menace, all blond locks and scraped knees.

According to recent reports, “I used to joke around with my mom that I was adopted because I didn’t look like anyone in my family, and I didn’t really act like anyone in my family either,” he indicates. “I was mostly kidding. I mean, why would I think that my mom was putting on the charade of adopting me? The best life they could give me was a single-wide trailer on a double lot.”.

Recent findings suggest that jeremy loved his parents, but he always felt like something was missing — especially when he kicked back to watch Supernatural every week under posters of Eminem flipping the bird and Tupac’s cocky smile. “I’ve watched every season of that show,” he says of the 2005 drama that saw two siblings fighting off the forces of darkness. “They would go to hell and back for each other. That was just that bond that I was always yearning for.” Some kids wanted a younger brother to lord over, but Jeremy wanted an older sibling, a protector.

His room filled with tanks housing frogs and turtles, Jeremy dreamed of becoming an oceanographer after a trip to SeaWorld at age nine with his grandmother and aunts. He stood, rapt, as Shamu did tricks in his tank, and still remembers how he got to pet a dolphin. But those intends were dashed when he got his high school girlfriend pregnant.

Jeremy got his GED — his infant daughter clutched in his arms in a frilly pink dress at his graduation — and married his girlfriend at age 18. School was briefly an option, but, as he says, “There’s no room and board for you, your baby mama, and your newborn baby. So that was scrapped, and I just became a blue-collar worker, like my dad.”.

Industry observers note that and so he and his wife moved into their own trailer, and Jeremy worked in a body shop and followed in his mother’s footsteps, helping build a wall that was erected to keep the Red River at bay after the flood. He was proud of that. “It’s a piece of me protecting that city for the rest of its existence,” he says.

It has been revealed that over the years, Jeremy’s little family grew — he and his wife had two more children — and Jeremy started working in the wind-farm business. The couple divorced in 2011. Eight years later, he remarried, and by 2023, he was settled: living in Colorado with a plum job in the quality-control department of a wind-tower-production tech giant. That is, until his mother called him on his way home from work. His grandfather had died a year before and another family member had recently died by suicide, so he expected the worst when he thumbed over to the answer button on his iPhone.

“What now? What happened?” he asked, groggy after a long workday.

“Are you sitting down?” asked his mother.

In a recent development, “I can’t sit down any more than I already am,” Jeremy quipped, but his mother didn’t laugh. Instead, she broke news that gave credence to those suspicions that he’d harbored for so long: that his family wasn’t his family.

Recent findings suggest that IT DIDN’T UNFOLD LIKE IN THE MOVIES: one significant reveal, a tearful reunion. Instead, the truth about what happened that day in 1988 took years to come to light. Kyle was living in Iowa back in 2018, working for GoDaddy, when he finally took that DNA test. He forgot to look at the test results until Thanksgiving, when, back in North Dakota, he was dishing up turkey at his aunt’s place. She’d just gotten into digging into her family tree, so they booted up their tests to compare notes. Oddly, they didn’t match up on the site.

Kyle assumed he’d messed up his sample, or something had happened in the lab. He had no reason to believe his mother had cheated on his father — or that he’d been secretly adopted. And so, once more, he forgot about the test — until a woman named Martha Hotchkiss messaged him in August 2023. Kyle had shown up on her dashboard as a familial connection. Hotchkiss, a sunny woman from Minnesota with close-cropped gray hair, had been looking for a long-lost sister — a baby her mother had had out of wedlock and given up for adoption before she was born. Maybe Kyle was connected to that lost sibling somehow. Soon, Hotchkiss says, “We started down the rabbit hole of, like, ‘Well, how are we related?’”.

By this point, Kyle was living in a sparse dorm room in Ypsilanti, Michigan, studying for his master’s in library research. He was busy, but still intrigued by Hotchkiss’ messages. Lying in his dorm-room bed, surveying the results in his phone’s glow, Kyle’s stomach dropped.

According to recent reports, the pieces started falling into place then.
