He couldn’t think too much about the switch until he graduated — otherwise, he’d fall apart.

It has been revealed that after all, Kyle had already been reeling from the news for a few weeks now. Before Martha spoke to Liz, Kyle and his brother told their parents about the switch separately: Kyle called his father, Keith, and Darren took his mother, Evelyn, ice fishing on the Bylin Dam. “I’m not so good about talking about feelings, but I was sick,” Keith says. “I was angry.” Evelyn was more worried about Kyle than anything else. “My first thoughts were ‘Why didn’t Kyle tell me himself? And how is Kyle? How is he doing? How is he feeling about this?’”.

At that point, the families were still essentially strangers — as Kyle was reminded of when he spoke with Liz over Zoom for the first time. They may have had the same strong brow, dark eyes, and even similar glasses, but this was still his first time talking to the woman. “I described it as ‘Oh, what a nice lady from Minnesota,’” Kyle states of first talking to his birth mom. “I had no real kind of concrete connection.”.

IT ALL FINALLY FELT REAL WHEN the families met in person. Liz first spotted Kyle through her living-room picture window. He was tall, she thought — like her ex-husband. It was April 2025, and Kyle was in Minneapolis, where Liz lives now, for a research conference, so it seemed like a good time to meet in person. He’d gotten lost on the way and was a bit harried when he knocked on the door to her compact blue house, a tall apple tree shading the modest yard. When Liz answered, they settled on a handshake. A hug seemed too personal for someone she’d essentially just met, Liz thought.

Sources indicate that once Kyle entered the foyer, the two clicked. Kyle noted the University of Michigan blanket he’d given to Liz as a gift after they first spoke resting over the back of a rocking chair — from his alma mater — and Liz took him on a tour of her basement packed with books about computer science left behind by her father. Kyle felt a pang when he learned his biological grandfather had died long ago. He’d been the head of the main-frame computer department at the University of Minnesota, and Kyle couldn’t help but think what it would have been like to have a relative so plugged into his own interests, the conversations they would have had at holidays.

It has been revealed that as he and Liz sorted through photos, though, Kyle was thrilled to see himself reflected back in the faces of his lost family members. A nose there, the curve of a jaw there. He felt seen in a way he’d never had before. And after a hearty Midwestern meal of spaghetti and milk, the two finally hugged.

Kyle met his biological dad, Terry, that Thanksgiving when he went home to North Dakota to visit Keith. Climbing into Terry’s black diesel pickup, Kyle noted that they shared the same dark eyes. Terry was full of stories — how he raised hell as a kid, tearing through the countryside on snowmobiles, chasing girls. When the two pulled up in front of Texas Roadhouse to have lunch, Kyle gave Terry an appraising look.

In a recent development, “You know, Terry,” he said, “you probably held me back at the hospital, at least once.” Terry, the outgoing chatterbox, went quiet then. Terry is stoic now, talking about the revelation that he’d missed out on all those years with Kyle. “There’s nothing I can do about it. I just got to start accepting it for what it is now,” he states. “As I said [to Kyle’s dad], ‘Well, Keith, we’ll come out of this with an extra boy, and we got each other as a friend.’”.

AFTER LIZ BROKE THE NEWS TO JEREMY, he called his father, Terry, while the older man was on the way to Fargo for supplies. “It’s hard to put it in words. There was disbelief at first,” Terry claims now. “I went home [from the hospital] thinking I had Jeremy Morrison.”.

In a recent development, it took Jeremy a few months to call Evelyn, his birth mother. Pacing between the hallway and bathroom, he peppered her with questions: Where was she from? What did she do for work? What was her favorite food? Evelyn noted that Jeremy laughed — and spoke — just like her son, Darren. Keith, who’d started therapy after the reveal, was just as nervous when he and Jeremy got on the phone. Still, Jeremy put him at ease; Jeremy and Kyle hadn’t grown up that far apart, so Keith and his biological son knew people in common in the farming world. As it turned out, Keith had had beers with Jeremy’s uncle more than once over the years — he’d even bought equipment from the man. And Keith told Jeremy all about Darren; it turns out the two men had basically the same car as teens, and both filled their rooms with fish tanks full of amphibians.

Jeremy saw his biological mother for the first time through the stucco windows of a chain Mexican restaurant in Grand Forks, North Dakota, in 2024. Sitting next to his wife, a basket of chips already on the table, he watched as a woman with cropped gray hair and his eyes walked up to the door. Evelyn recognized the man right away; even dressed in camo shorts, an arm full of tattoos, he looked just like her son Darren. They hugged, and Jermey’s wife took pictures, then sat down to eat — and talk. Jeremy doesn’t want to share what they discussed — it’s too personal — but he does say that “her independence, her stubbornness, her quick wit — yeah, I definitely got that from her.” It’s true: Both are quick to a wry joke; both have a way with words befitting a natural storyteller.

Recent findings suggest that the next day, Jeremy made the hour-plus drive to the Bylin farm. As he pulled up in front of the big white house, the fields rippling with barley, soybeans, and sunflowers — cows long gone — Jeremy took note of the lake. He imagined himself playing hockey on the frozen surface during the winter, fishing in the summer heat. Keith was just beginning to set up for a Fourth of July potluck, dragging out tables and chairs onto the lawn, when he saw Jeremy walking toward him in jeans and a tank top reading “Wake Up and Smell the Freedom” in patriotic colors.

Sources indicate that “To actually see him walk up to me, it’s kind of like seeing somebody come from the dead,” Keith notes. “He just looks like my older son. He’s got the same walk. They got the same mustache.” Darren was supposed to attend the celebration, but ducked out at the last minute, overwhelmed by the prospect of meeting a brother he’d never known. In some ways, Keith says, the whole ordeal has been hardest on Darren, caught up in a circus he’s only tangentially a part of.

In a recent development, jeremy and Darren did eventually meet up, a year later at the same Mexican joint he and Evelyn ate at, but neither wanted to talk much about what they discussed. “This is a mess that has affected many people in a confusing, sad, depressing way. The butterfly effect is endless,” Darren mentioned in a statement to Rolling Stone after declining an interview. “No wonder Kyle and I have always been on such different paths in life. I was never able to look through his eyes and understand much. I sometimes wonder how the farm would look positively with a brother involved.”.

AS THE FAMILIES SLOWLY GET TO KNOW each other, Keith can’t stop wondering what happened in the hospital all those years ago. Were the babies switched on purpose? And if so, why? Was it a mistake? The boys were the only babies in the hospital that day, according to local news — that week, even — so how, and when, did the switch occur?

Sources indicate that near misses and switches are apparently not as uncommon as one might think, according to experts. “We assume it’s extremely rare because the only cases we hear about are those that are detected,” states psychologist Nancy Segal, co-author of Accidental Brothers: The Story of Twins Exchanged at Birth and the Power of Nature and Nurture. She cites a study that estimates that 20,000 accidental baby switches happen per year, but most are corrected before the babies go home. “Not all such cases are ever going to be discovered,” Segal adds. “There are some that probably are never detected, and then some that may be discovered but never reported. I suspect they are more common than we think.”.

Statistics aside, both families wanted answers, so Evelyn hunted down a lawyer who would take their case against the hospital. They filed a lawsuit back in July, suing for negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress, deceit, and medical malpractice. They’re asking for damages for “past and future pain, inconvenience … mental anguish, emotional distress, and other non-pecuniary damages,” according to the suit.

The hospital answered the lawsuit, denying any negligence and claiming that “defendants are without knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to the truth of the allegations.”.

It has been revealed that when asked for comment, the hospital responded: “We are currently working to better understand a highly unusual situation involving two men who apparently were separated from their biological parents at some point during their lives…. We recognize the profound impact this discovery has had on them and their families. Unfortunately, because of the passage of nearly four decades, the medical and staffing records that might have provided additional clarity no longer exist, and no members of the delivery team from that time are still employed by the hospital. While we deeply sympathize with the men and their families, we have found no evidence to support claims that Unity Medical Center or its staff were responsible for what occurred.”.

Meanwhile, Keith has been sleuthing. After the lawsuit hit local news, he heard from two other women who claim they had near misses at the same hospital. One gave birth at Unity in December 1971. “We were about to leave, and [the nurse] had brought me this baby,” indicates one woman, who declined to be identified due to privacy reasons. “My baby was a smaller baby, and this baby was pretty plump. I stated, ‘This is not my baby.’”.

Industry observers note that another had her own mixup in June 1975. “I got out of bed and got in my chair, and [a nurse] handed me my baby,” states the second woman, who also asked to remain anonymous. “I was just trying to get the baby to latch, and this nurse came just hustling back into the room and remarked, ‘That’s not your baby.’ Would I have noticed it days later? No, I probably wouldn’t have. It was back in the days where I was having a very difficult delivery, and they gave me ether.”.

Lawyers for the hospital did not respond to questions regarding these claims.

Despite the drama, the legal battle, the meshing of two very different families, Kyle and Jeremy are still finding bright moments. Evelyn and Keith are getting to know Jeremy’s kids, and Kyle is getting closer to Liz. He even visited Martha and Liz in Minnesota over the summer, relaxing by Lake Michigan and exploring the sand dunes surrounding it. Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years.

And the parents are bonding, too. Last Christmas, Liz pulled Kyle aside during a visit to Minnesota and, under the festive lights, told him Keith had done a great job raising him. When he heard that, Keith — the self-described stoic — cried.

According to recent reports, and then there’s Jeremy and Kyle — those very different kids who grew up into very different men living each other’s lives. They don’t talk much now (unless it’s about the lawsuit), don’t live near each other, and don’t have much in common — except for trauma. There’s no real word for what they are to each other; they’re still figuring that out. They’re not brothers, they’re not related, but they are intertwined in a way that’s hard to ignore. Their pasts are linked, and, now, their futures are, too.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (881 w)

There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another tech giant is having an outage.
  • According to recent reports, that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another tech giant is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

According to recent reports, that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Industry observers note that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Industry observers note that mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find fresh security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be mentioned for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Sources indicate that barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as promptly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one firm, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

In a recent development, of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Hisense 65M7SR probably won't win any spec-sheet battles, but for what it costs, that won't matter. Its Mini-LED picture looked great across every piece of content I threw at it, Roku's interface is a joy to use as always, and it handled casual gaming without a hitch. If you can grab one on sale, it’s an absolute steal.

Vivid, colorful Mini-LED picture for the money.

Dolby Vision support at a budget price.

Slim design that doesn't scream "budget TV".

60Hz panel and HDMI 2.0 ports limit high FPS gaming.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Industry observers note that mini-LED used to be something you paid a premium for. Now, it's showing up on the best TVs that cost less than a weekend trip. The Hisense 65M7SR is a prime example of that: a 65-inch Mini-LED TV with Dolby Vision, Roku's famously streamlined interface, and a list price of $699.99 that I wouldn't expect anyone to actually pay (it’s on sale often for as low as $399.99).

Industry observers note that this is Hisense's entry point into Mini-LED, so it makes a couple of trade-offs to hit that price, namely a 60Hz panel and HDMI 2.0 port setup. I spent some time with the 65-inch model, watching shows on Netflix, soaking in 4K videos on YouTube, and playing a couple of PlayStation 5 games, and I came away much more impressed than I expected. The 65M7SR won’t dazzle anyone on paper, but in my real-world tests, it held its own very well.

Industry observers note that the Hisense 65M7SR launched in September 2026 and comes in a handful of sizes. Here's how the lineup breaks down:.

• Hisense 50M7SR (50-inch): $499.99.

• Hisense 55M7SR (55-inch): $549.99.

• Hisense 65M7SR (65-inch): $699.99.

• Hisense 75M7SR (75-inch): $899.99.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

• Hisense 85M7SR (85-inch): $1,299.99.

According to recent reports, that $699.99 sticker price is more of a suggestion at this point. I've seen the 65-inch model drop to just $399.99 more than once, and that's the price I’d expect to see it at for some time (still, snag one swiftly if you absolutely want to lock in that discount). At $700, there are better TVs out there than the 65M7SR, but at $400, I think the purchase makes a lot more sense.

Dolby Vision, HDR 10, Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG).

3 x HDMI 2.0, 1 x LAN, 1 x Optical digital audio, 1 x USB-A 2.0.

Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth, Apple AirPlay 2.

56.9 x 34.6 x 11.7 (w/ stand); 56.9 x 33 x 2.6 in (w/o stand).

The 65M7SR sticks to the budget TV design playbook, but it pulls it off with a little more polish than I expected. The bezels are slim, the frame has a simple flat black, and the whole thing measures just 2.6 inches deep, so it won't look bulky on a stand or mounted on the wall. Without the stand, it weighs 38.4 pounds, so moving it around is pretty easy.

The 65M7SR sticks to the budget TV design playbook, but it pulls it off with a little more polish than I expected.

If you'd rather set it on furniture, the included feet can be placed in two different configurations: sitting out toward the edges of the screen, or closer to the center. I like keeping them at the center because they take up less space and are compatible with more media setups. That’s why center pedestal stands will always be best in my eyes, but this style comes in at a close second. It's a clean, no-frills look, and I mean that as a compliment.

The 65M7SR has three HDMI ports, all of which are HDMI 2.0 (that, coupled with the fact that its refresh rate of 60Hz means is not going to make the list of our best gaming TVs. ). Still, one of them supports eARC, so you can hook up a soundbar without sacrificing an input. Beyond that, you get a USB-A port, Ethernet, optical digital audio out, and a cable/antenna input.

Recent findings suggest that three HDMI ports are plenty for most setups, though if you've got a soundbar, a console, and a Blu-ray player, you'll fill them up quickly. Another thing to note: the 65M7SR doesn’t support Bluetooth, so you can't pair wireless devices directly with the TV. That's a bummer, but I don’t feel it’s a deal-breaker at this price.

I started my testing with "East of Eden" on Netflix, and the picture looked great right away. Colors were rich, and skin tones looked natural compared to the overcooked look that many budget TVs fall victim to. SDR brightness is a strength here (the 65M7SR hit 466 nits in our testing, the highest in the test results table below), so the image stayed punchy and easy to see even with the lights on. Dolby Vision support (which is rare on a TV at this price) made the whole experience feel more cinematic than I expected.

Next up was "Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2," also on Netflix, and it might have been my favorite stretch of the whole test. The show's neon-soaked city is basically a stress test for color, and the 65M7SR handled it with ease. Signs and lights popped against the dark backdrops, and the fast-moving action scenes stayed crisp and smooth.

Input latency (in milliseconds).

Sources indicate that for our technical tests, we use a Jeti spectraval 1501-HiRes spectroradiometer, a Klein K10-A colorimeter, a Murideo 8K-SIX-G Metal pattern generator, and Portrait Displays’ Calman TV calibration software to take measurements. We also use a Leo Bodnar 4K Input Lag Tester for determining whether it’s one of the best gaming TVs.

Subjective tests vary based on the reviewer, but usually feature anecdotes from a diverse selection of movies, TV shows, and other content reflecting the types of things you may actually want to watch on the TV.

For a more detailed look at what we do and how we do it, check out our “How we test TVs” page.

Recent findings suggest that netflix’s "Grand Theft Auto VI Extended Look” looked just as good, with sharp detail and plenty of pop. The detail in the sun-bleached streets and the saturated sunsets came through clearly, though this is where the TV showed some of its limits. It peaked at just 463 nits in our HDR tests, which is the lowest in our results table, so don't expect searing highlights. I never felt like I was missing out while watching, but a brighter set like the Hisense U6SF Pro will make HDR content look a lot brighter. The TCL QM64L is another strong budget pick for HDR brightness at 630 nits and a great Amazon-Vega-OS-based alternative to the 65M7SR.

According to recent reports, I also threw on some 4K nature videos on YouTube to see how the TV handles real-world detail, and they looked great. Foliage, water, and wildlife were richly detailed, and the colors were lively without being overly saturated or cartoonish. Color accuracy isn't the 65M7SR's strongest suit with a Delta-E of 3.05, but I didn't see anything that looked off, and its 95.16% UHDA-P3 coverage gives it plenty of range.

Gaming performance is solid for the price. I played some of "Marvel's Spider-Man 2" and "Marvel's Wolverine" on a PlayStation 5 to test the TV's gaming features, and both looked and felt great. Game Mode Plus and ALLM kept things feeling snappy, and VRR support helped keep the action smooth.

Sources indicate that the 65M7SR's 13.8ms input lag is slightly higher than that of the other TVs in the results table, but I couldn't notice it at all. Swinging through Manhattan still looked gorgeous, and Wolverine's fast-paced brawls felt responsive from start to finish. The one catch is that the 60Hz panel and HDMI 2.0 ports mean you won't get the 120Hz modes that some games offer, so if you want that, you'll need to spend more.

According to recent reports, the 65M7SR's built-in speakers are a 20W, two-channel setup, and they get the job done well enough. Dialogue came through clearly, which is the most key thing for a TV like this, but big moments, like the action scenes in "Wolverine," could use more punch and low-end weight than a pair of stock budget TV speakers can provide.

The fix is the same as it is for just about every TV: get one of the best soundbars. Luckily, the eARC-enabled HDMI port makes pairing one easy, so you can upgrade your audio without much hassle.

Recent findings suggest that the 65M7SR runs Roku OS, and it's still the interface I'd pick over most others. The home screen is free of clutter (mostly), finding something to watch is painless, and every major streaming app is right there waiting for you. You also get support for Apple AirPlay, Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home.

Roku's home screen still has a fair number of ads, and you'll notice them. But compared to the busier layouts on many competing TVs, it's easy to live with. If you want minimalism in your OS, Roku remains at the top of the pack.

According to recent reports, the 65M7SR comes with the basic Roku remote, and it does exactly what you'd want it to do. It has a voice button for hands-free searching, dedicated buttons for popular streaming services, and a layout so straightforward that you could hand it to a guest, and they'd figure it out in seconds. It also has a relatively small form factor, which is great news if you’re averse to bulky peripherals (not so great if you often lose your remote, though).

It has been revealed that the Hisense 65M7SR is a great pick for anyone looking to step up to Mini-LED for a low price. It delivers a vivid, colorful picture, smooth, responsive gaming, and Roku's excellent interface at a price you just can't beat. The 60Hz panel, HDMI 2.0 ports, and underwhelming speakers keep it from a perfect score, but none of them ruined my time with it.

If you want a faster 144Hz panel and HDMI 2.1 ports for gaming, look to the Hisense U6SF Pro, though it usually runs a couple hundred dollars more. If you're comparing it to other budget Mini-LED sets, the Hisense QD7 and Vizio VQM65C are both worth a look, too. The TCL QM64L is another good budget Mini-LED pick if you prefer Amazon’s Vega OS to Roku’s. But if you want an easy, great-looking TV that won't drain your wallet, the Hisense 65M7SR should absolutely be on your shortlist. Just do yourself a favor, and make sure you get it on sale.

Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, stated last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

According to recent reports, in fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

It has been revealed that the law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

#142717. The 200 Best Songs of the 1990s

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4768 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollingstone ↗ Open Full Page

The 200 Best Songs of the 1990s

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Nineties music explosion was a golden age.
  • Sources indicate that so let’s break it down: the 200 best songs of the Nineties.
  • It has been revealed that this list has so many legends: Nirvana, Biggie, Prince, Madonna, the Wu-Tang Clan, Radiohead, Oasis, Jay-Z, OutKast, Garth, Whitney, Alanis, Aaliyah.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Nineties music explosion was a golden age. Whatever style of music rings your bells, it was booming in the Nineties — from grunge to gangsta rap, from country to techno, from riot-grrrl punk to TRL teen-pop. It was the age of Lollapalooza and Lilith Fair, Kurt and Courtney, Biggie and Tupac, Beavis and Butt-Head. Fans were devouring music—paying actual money for CDs! in record stores! — on a level never seen before or since. We felt stupid and contagious. It was the most gloriously chaotic era for music ever — which is why so many fans revere as the greatest.

Sources indicate that so let’s break it down: the 200 best songs of the Nineties. The hits, the misses, the deep cults, the fan favorites. A mix tape of pop classics, rockers, rappers, soul divas, disco jams, country twangers, punk ragers, dance-floor anthems, karaoke standards. There’s all-time legends and one-hit wonders. But only one song per artist, or half the list would be Missy Elliott.

It has been revealed that this list has so many legends: Nirvana, Biggie, Prince, Madonna, the Wu-Tang Clan, Radiohead, Oasis, Jay-Z, OutKast, Garth, Whitney, Alanis, Aaliyah. There’s rising pop stars ready to conquer the next century, like Beyoncé and Britney; there’s also grizzled vets like Bob Dylan and Neil Young, refusing to fade away. There’s Latest Jack Swing, Britpop, trip-hop, shoegaze, ska, goth, rave. And Cher, obviously.

Some of these Nineties songs remain famous around the world. You hear them at weddings, parties, clubs, the karaoke bar. Others make people run and scream in terror. Some are cult classics that only the hardcore fans know. Every fan would make a different list — that’s the whole greatness of it. There’s no way one list could sum up such a bountiful decade.

But all 200 of these tunes reflect the beauty, the brilliance, the weirdness of Nineties music. Slip this mix tape into your boombox, crank up the volume, and press play.

Paul Natkin/Wire Image; Al Pereira/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images; Paul Bergen/Redferns/Getty Images; Dave Hogan/Getty Images; Brian Rasic/Getty Images; Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic; Steve Granitz/WireImage; Gie Knaeps/Getty Images; Ron Davis/Getty Images; Tim Mosenfelder/Getty Images; Lester Cohen/Getty Images; Steve Eichner/Getty Images; Frank Micelotta/Getty Images; Chris Walter/WireImage.

According to recent reports, the Bay Area rap crew Digital Underground kicked off the Nineties with that rarest of pop treasures — the song that absolutely everybody loves. “The Humpty Dance” was the summer jam of 1990, as the late great Shock G turned into his crazed alter ego Humpty Hump. His motto: “I’m a freak! I like the girls with the boom! I once got busy in a Burger King bathroom!”  As Shock G said, “I wanted to bring the gap between Prince and hip-hop.” Digital Underground were a free-spirited collective where the freaks were definitely welcome. (Tupac got his start as a member.)  “The Humpty Dance” remains a timeless dance-floor banger—and the perfect song to get this party started right. R.I.P., Humpty Hump. All over America, Burger King employees are still mopping up after you.

Recent findings suggest that A brazen Australian punk queen and her shy guitar boy, after nearly a decade of small-time scuffling, finally conquer America with “I Touch Myself,” the most shamelessly sticky-fingered ode to solo sex to ever hit the Top Ten. Every other autoerotic jam out there sounded coy and simpy compared to this, especially since Christina Amphlett sings it with all her vixen energy. (Somehow “Shock the Monkey” never hit like this.) “I like double entendres,” she said, but come on — “I Touch Myself” barely counts as half an entendre, which is why it’s brilliant.

Third Eye Blind’s hits always stood out because of Stephan Jenkins’ sore thumb of a voice — sharp, pushy, adenoidal, so bitchy you wondered if he was kidding, except he never was. But his narcissistic flash was a breath of fresh air, as rock radio recovered from its Her Placenta Falls To the Floor phase. In “Semi-Charmed Life,” he’s bedeviled by a woman who just uses him for his body (a frequent Stephan Jenkins dilemma, at least in his songs) and leaves him doing way too many drugs (ditto), to that “doo doo doo” chorus.

It has been revealed that latest York club-kid DJ culture, translated into a Saturday-morning kiddie cartoon? This groove really is in the heart, as Lady Miss Kier holds court alongside her Ukrainian DJ (Dimitry) and a Japanese art student (Towa Tei), meeting up to form their own world clique. This party has everything: a very young Q-Tip rapping in a “Hendrix haze,” Bootsy Collins on bass (“Dig!”), soul horns from the legends Maceo Parker and Fred Wesley, a jazz bassline sampled from Herbie Hancock, hooks swiped from Dr. Seuss and the Beatles. But Deee-Lite turn their global collage aesthetic into a timeless disco floor-filler.

Remember those weekends when your mom would lock herself in the bathroom for “Bible study” after asking to borrow some AA batteries? It was all Seal’s fault. This man was the smoothest of romantic balladeers, and he proves it in “Kiss from a Rose.” The words make absolutely no sense at all (“Did you know when it snows, my eyes become large?” No, Seal, in fact we did not) but he turns anything he sings into pillow talk. You can hear how hard he works at singing the word “baaay-baaay” exactly like George Michael in “Faith,” and these are the tiny details classic slow jams are made of..

Sources indicate that stephen Merritt burrowed through the Nineties, making his name as one of the most clever songwriters around. But he took everyone by surprise with his triple-disc opus 69 Love Songs. He’d already crafted so many gems with the Magnetic Fields, Future Bible Heroes, and the 6ths. (Their 1995 Wasps’ Nests is a real spinner, especially when Barbara Manning sings “San Diego Zoo.”) “All My Little Words” is his most exquisitely despondent ballad with singer Dudley Klute lamenting, “I could make you fly away, but I could never make you stay.” Even the banjo sounds miserable.

Recent findings suggest that few songs could capture the blissed-out poetics of hip-hop circa 1994 like the greatest hit by Keith Murray, one of the coolest MCs ever to go by his government name. “The Most Beautifullest Thing In This World” is laid-back, cozy like a blanket, as Murray kicks it in the basement with Erick Sermon and Redman, getting interplanetarian like Doctor Who.

According to recent reports, the Verve’s Richard Ashcroft was born to be a rock star: 40 per cent lips, 40 per cent cheekbones, 20 per cent shades, until he opened his mouth and became 100 per cent poetic pretensions. In the great tradition of English bands, the Verve hated each other so much they broke up every time they made an album. “Bittersweet Symphony” is their classic, with Mad Richard at his most shamanic. They famously lost the rights by sampling an orchestral remake of the Rolling Stones’ “The Last Time.” (A gospel standard the Stones had no business claiming as an original in the first place) But “Bittersweet Symphony” was the hit that made them international superstars. Naturally, they immediately broke up.

Industry observers note that butt of course. At the height of the “never trust a big butt and a smile” era, Sir Mix-A-Lot was there to remind us all to always — always — trust butt.

Industry observers note that pam Tillis was one of the era’s unforgettable country voices, with classics like “Maybe It Was Memphis” and “Spilled Perfume,” giving us so many poignant ballads. This is NOT one of them. “Cleopatra, Queen of Denial” is a high-water mark of the Nineties Hot Country line-dance boom, with the great Nashville goofball song title of the decade. (A close second: Mark Chesnutt’s “Bubba Shot the Jukebox.”) “He’s probably stuck in traffic/He’ll be here in a little while / Just call me Cleopatra, everybody, because I’m the Queen of Denial.”.

A landmark of French filter-house, not to mention a prime Nile Rodgers rip from an era full of them. Daft Punk’s Thomas Bangalter (he’s the robot on the left, or maybe the one on the right, who knows) did this one-off collabo with a couple of club confreres, bouncing the simple refrain off an energy-flash guitar lick (sampled from a Chaka Khan record) to the break of dawn.

The ultimate New Jack Swing smooch ballad. The early Nineties were a golden age for teen R&B slow jams, from smoothies like Mint Condition or Color Me Badd. The Waco, Texas boys in Hi-Five were the deep South’s answer to New Edition, with hits such as “I Like the Way (The Kissing Game).” But “I Can’t Wait Another Minute” is prom perfection, as the boys harmonize to pour their hearts out, before the clock ticks down to curfew.

A haunting love story, from the Spinanes’ guitar poet Rebecca Gates, one of the era’s sharpest indie-rock storytellers. Gates sings about a romance from the past, going through old photos, postcards, love letters. She plays an old mix tape, remembering how much you loved that song by the Verlaines. But even though she knows the relationship didn’t work — “it’s my heart and it doesn’t fit yours” — the memory of that song won’t leave her alone. “Hawaiian Baby” is a springtime song for sure—every April I lose at least one day disappearing into this tune.

According to recent reports, A Wu-Tang family affair: Ghostface gives it up to his mama with a gospel choir and a string section. “All That I Got Is You” is a vulnerable confession amid the bravado ofIronman, as Ghost looks back on the struggle of growing up in the desperate poverty of the Staten Island projects, where he had to “pluck roaches out of the cereal box” and wonder why he was ever born at all. Mary J. Blige sweetens the song in the voice of the angel showing him the way forward.

According to recent reports, just another bunch of Orange County punk dudes going megaplatinum with a ditty about masochism. The Offspring had quite a run of grunge bangers after emerging from the SoCal hardcore scene, with “Come Out and Play (Keep ‘Em Separated)” and “Why Don’t You Get a Job?” But “Self Esteem” is their funniest and best, with the quintessential Nineties proverb, “I might be dumb but I’m not a dweeb.” It’s still a timely sentiment—unless you ARE a dumb dweeb, in which case you’re probably the guy in this song.

Trying to pick just one song from the Clueless soundtrack? That’s as useless as searching for meaning in a Pauly Shore movie.

Recent findings suggest that the former Menudo stud shook his bon-bon to the electric-salsa sleaze of “Livin’ La Vida Loca,” falling under the spell of a mocha seductress with devil-red lips. Ricky’s popularity took a tumble after his disastrous dance with President George W. Bush, but he hung in there, eventually came out, and got his shot at redemption in American Crime Story: The Assassination of Gianni Versace.

According to recent reports, kate Pierson and Cindy Wilson take it hip to hip, rocketing through the wilderness. The B-52s looked like a thing of the past, after the death of their guitar savant Ricky Wilson, but the Georgia latest wavers took their grief and danced this mess around, when Cosmic Thing blew up as their surprise comeback hit. “Roam” feels like an elegy for Ricky, but it soars like an invitation to a Southern road trip, as Kate and Cindy go for a spin down the dirty back roads of their memories.

Recent findings suggest that A Detroit techno classic from the legend Carl Craig, one of dance music’s most innovative minds. “Throw” is a classic from his alter ego Paperclip People, with disco vocals distorted into the stratosphere, eerie robot synths, planet-rocking bass throb. LCD Soundsystem do a bang-up version of “Throw” live. Carl Craig learned to play guitar at 15, as he said, “because I wanted to be Prince.” But then he heard his lifelong heroes Kraftwerk. “I threw all that Prince shit out the window. I wanted to be Kraftwerk.” “Throw” came from touring England with fellow Detroit techno pioneers Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, inspired by the raves.“I put out ‘Throw’ in 1994,” Craig recalled. “I played it on acetate at a small club and the floor jumped. That was how it all started.”.

According to recent reports, A buried treasure from Dump — the sound of a sad guitar boy in his room, pouring his heart into his 4-track. He plays a bittersweet melody on his guitar, stretching it out, letting it build for 10, 11, 12 minutes of achingly plaintive rock shimmer, with a Brian Wilson sense of pathos. Then he signs off with a coda where he warbles a few lines about flying away and waving goodbye. The boy is James McNew, bassist for Yo La Tengo, but auteur behind excellent Dump records like this 10-inch vinyl EP, or his Prince covers album The Skinny Motherfucker with the High Voice. The Nineties underground was full of DIY songwriters like this, making their music not to get rich or popular or even heard, but just to get their feelings down on tape for a few minutes. “International Airport” might be the most obscure song on this list, but once heard, it’s in your soul forever.

It has been revealed that ten years after his debut, Ladies Loved Cool James more than ever. In “Doin’ It,” he represents Queens, she was raised out in Brooklyn, but neither of them is getting any sleep. LL brings in his fellow Eighties O.G. rapper LeShaun to reprise her “doin’ it, doin’ it, doin’ it well” hook, for one of the Nineties’ friendliest sex songs. Uncle L was already a rap veteran heading into the 1990s—he began the decade proclaiming, “Don’t call it a comeback!” But when he dropped “Doin’ It” in 1996, it was downright shocking how he’d managed to stay on top for so long without ever going stale. He calls this hit his personal favorite — as he recently remarked, “I think the beat, the lyric, the flow, the collaboration, the moment, the visual — it’s perfect.”.

All they wanna do is zoom-a-zoom zoom-zoom and a boom-boom, over those Teddy Riley beats.

Everything But the Girl started in the Eighties as a moody New Wave duo, a married couple with a taste for cocktail jazz and bossa nova. But they grew up with a bang in the Nineties, with the acoustic folk-soul breakthrough Amplified Heart. Then things got weird: “Missing” blew up into a left-field pop hit, in a dance remix by Todd Terry. EBTG kept exploring club beats on Walking Wounded and Temperamental, but “Missing” is their deepest cry from the heart, as Tracey Thorn and Ben Watt grieve over a loss that won’t heal.

A true only-in-the-Nineties hit, from the moment when electronica went populist. An English techno DJ digs up an obscure hippie-gospel hook, then bombards it with go-go breakbeats and computer blurps and Nashville honky-tonk piano. Result? A pop smash everybody and their mother loves. Norman Cook, a.k.a Fatboy Slim, mixed a whole armful of rare wax — most prominently, Camille Yarborough’s voice—into a song that sounded at home in a club, a minivan, a day-care center, a druggy rave, or a dollar-an-hour Internet café. It summed up the genre briefly dubbed “big beat,” one of the most useless names any genre has ever had. At other points in history, “Praise You” would have been considered a weird little art project. But in the anything-goes Nineties, it was pure pop for all people.

Industry observers note that cornershop took the guitar drone of the Velvet Underground somewhere new in this uplifting processional hymn, sung entirely in Punjabi. Tjinder Singh and his brother Avtar were London guys with Indian parents, taking their band name from the English stereotype of Indian immigrants managing convenience stores. (They even put out their DIY debut on “curry-colored” vinyl.) “Jullander Shere” is a guitar groove mixing up sitar, tablas, a stoner electro-rave vibe, devotional vocals, for six jubilant minutes. (Very rough translation: “Brothers and sisters, we are speaking of the true path!”) Cornershop went on to have hits like “Brimful of Asha,” working that same groove.

Hey ho, let’s go: “Slam” is one massive mosh pit of grimy Queens hip-hop and hardcore punk, with a room full of crowd-surfing, body-smashing, slap-happy hooligans. “We wanted to bring slam dancing to rap,” Onyx’s Fredro Starr mentioned. “Believe it or not, Nirvana was a big influence on us. Red Hot Chili Peppers too.” The baldhead rappers got massive with this jock jam, from their well-titled Bacdafucup. Their awesomely tone-deaf singing has a jolly all-in-together-now spirit, even if Onyx were out of their minds on acid when they recorded it.

In the wide-open days of the Nineties, practically anything could explode into a hit, no matter how bizarre. Exhibit A: the English techno duo Utah Saints, who scored a global arena-rave smash with “Something Good.” At first, they’re shouting their remarkably silly name. (“Utah Saints! U-U-U-Utah Saints!”) But the disco beats build until they get to the climax—a sample of Kate Bush singing exactly one line, from her hit “Cloudbursting”: “Ooooooh, I just KNOW that something good is gonna happen!” They warp her voice, looping the line over and over until it turns into a glow-stick mantra. By the end, the idea of turning Kate Bush into a disco diva sounds like a stroke of genius, taking her to wuthering newly introduced heights. “Something Good” snagged more airplay in the 1990s than all of her actual music combined, yet nobody was mad at it. No wonder Kate herself loved it.

The Tejano queen became a permanent pop legend even though her life ended tragically too soon, at her musical peak. “Fotos y Recuerdos” highlights off her eclectic style — a Spanish-language cumbia version of the Pretenders’s fresh wave nugget “Back on the Chain Gang.” It was Top Five on the Billboard Latin charts the week Selena died, becoming her first posthumous Number One.

Usher, still in his teens, makes his significant move with his breakthrough hit, agonizing over a love triangle, torn apart by doubt and guilt. “You Make Me Wanna…” introduced Usher as we’ve known him ever since.

Sources indicate that suede helped kick off the Britpop explosion, which gave us a sizable percentage of the decade’s kickiest guitar bands, with champs like Pulp, Blur, Elastica, Oasis, Placebo, the Auteurs, but also fondly remembered fly-by-nighters like Shed Seven, Gene, and Menswe@r. It couldn’t have happened without Suede, who threw down the gauntlet for everyone with their debut single “The Drowners.” The London boys turn their Bowie/Roxy obsessions into a glam-trash manifesto, with hair-flopping madman Brett Anderson yelping, “We kiss in his room to a popular tune!”.

Recent findings suggest that people were just starting to say “empowerment” as the Nineties began and sick of it by Y2K, but the concept was pretty much defined by Nineties R&B radio. Case in point: Deborah Cox’s “Nobody’s Supposed To Be Here,” a rainy-day jam about a woman who’s gotten burned too many times but dares to try again. (“How…did…you…GET here?” Damn.) First it was a blockbuster ballad, then got remixed into a disco hit—both versions killed. When Angela Bassett directed her Lifetime biopic about Whitney Houston, Ms. Cox had the honor of singing Whitney’s vocals.

Paul got his mojo in the Nineties—he stopped aiming for mainstream pop hits, and started trusting his eccentric muse again. “Calico Skies” is a poignant acoustic ballad from Flaming Pie, with finger-picking straight from the White Album. It feels like a love song to Linda under the shadow of mortality, with Paul vowing, “I’ll hold you for the rest of my life,” just a year before she passed away from cancer. “Calico Skies” was one of the songs played at her memorial service, in Paul’s string arrangement for the Brodsky Quartet.

In a recent development, tori Amos came on like one of rock’s truest rock eccentrics — she aspired to be as huge as Zeppelin or the Stones, straddling her piano bench. “Cornflake Girl” was her parable of growing up in America, set amid the cryptic battle of Cornflake Girls vs. Raisin Girls, with Tori gulping, “Rabbit, where’d you put the keys, girl?” The success of “Cornflake Girl” put Amos in a position where she was primed for mainstream stardom — all she had to do was, you know, maybe tone it down a notch? Needless to say, that’s when she entered her “breast-feeding a pig in the album photos” era.

According to recent reports, A psychedelic R&B slow jam from Mya, the D.C. ingenue who spent her nineteenth summer in the Top Ten with her very first single, “It’s All About Me.” Mya sings uncannily like Prince’s feminine alter ego Camille, her voice lost in dubbed-out reverb, with help from Dru Hill’s Sisqo (pre-“Thong Song”) and producer Darryl Pearson, as she kicks her groovy sexual politics: “Tonight it’s about me, me, me, me, me / Forget about you, you, you, you, you.”.

Yep, what a concept. The San Jose golf bros in Smash Mouth might have looked like a one-shot fluke after their 1997 hit “Walkin’ on the Sun,” but “All Star” was a jock-rock pep talk, as the late Steve Harwell reminds us all that you’ll never shine if you don’t glow.

“Da Dip” was one of the Dirty South’s easiest dance crazes: “I put my hand up on your hip/ When I dip, you dip, we dip!” Even Cardi B busted these New Orleans moves in “Bodak Yellow.” The B-side was called “Bump That Rump.”.

And now, dear reader, I fear it’s time for some tough love. As we used to say back in the Nineties, this is a “care-frontation.” You probably believe “Hold On” is the best Wilson Phillips song, right? So wrong. So tragically wrong. That’s fine for the locals, but true Wilson Phillips aficionados prize their real masterpiece, “You Won’t See Me Cry,” the over-the-top tearjerker ballad from their underrated 1992 follow-up album, complete with a flaming candelabra of a sax solo. For Carnie, Wendy, and Chynna, it’s their “Wouldn’t It Be Nice?”.

In a recent development, L’amour, c’est bleu. A bittersweet guitar-chime gem from one of the decade’s great cult indie-pop records, Ivy’s Apartment Life, whose mood is captured by the cover photo of a mod French girl putting on her makeup — glossy yet introspective. The dream-team trio features the late Andy Schlesinger (moonlighting from Fountains of Wayne), Andy Chase and chanteuse Dominique Durand, whose Parisienne accent adds that touch of tres tragique to their young-adult romantic malaise. “I’ve Got a Feeling” made a memorable appearance in the first episode of Felicity, but a melody this great would make an impression anywhere. If you’re living your life without this song, you’re blowing it significant-time.

The Chapel Hill scruffers Superchunk let out a rebel yell for Gen X kids with the day-job blues, for their wonderfully snotty breakthrough single — a punk rock “Take This Job and Shove It.” Mac McCaughan wrote it about an annoying co-worker at the copy shop. (Google “copy shops” — they were such a thing.) “Slack Motherfucker” sounded like a one-shot, but as it happened, Superchunk turned into one of the era’s most enduringly brilliant guitar bands, still going strong. A dumb Nineties joke: Why did the indie rocker cry? She moved to Chapel Hill and saw a sign that said “Merge Left.”.

Sources indicate that an anarchist punk anthem about fighting the power? A common-as-muck English working-class drinking song? A bizarro but beautiful fluke of a pop hit that never fails to light up any room? Guilty on all charges. “Tubthumping” remains a song for those days when you get knocked down, but you get up again.

The Glasgow cardigan kids won a worldwide audience without even trying. “Me and the Major” is a highlight of their breakthrough album If You’re Feeling Sinister, bristling with bookish wit, as Stuart Murdoch sings about a strange cross-generational friendship with an older guy who seems exotic to him. (“He remembers all the punks and the hippies too / And he remembers Roxy Music in ’72.”) But for Belle and Sebastian, this was just the beginning.

According to recent reports, the Upcoming Jersey duo P. M. Dawn had their own style of dreamy hip-hop reveries, aiming to sound soft and tender. “Set Adrift on Memory Bliss” turned into a startling Number One hit, with that jaw-dropping Spandau Ballet sample. The song mixed up Native Tongues-style hip-hop, New Romantic synth-pop, and goth melodrama. P.M. Dawn rejected rap cliches about gender roles, and paid the price for it, which might be why they’re so underrated now. But “Set Adrift” is a tribute to Prince Be’s omnivore imagination as well as his gentle warmth.

Sebadoh were an archetypal Nineties cult band—the guys who sang the tongue-in-cheek anthem “Gimme Indie Rock!” (Sample verse: “Milk that sound, blow your load/Further than you ever thought it would go/Four stars in the Rolling Stone!”) But in “Brand Fresh Love,” the punk wolfboys take a bold step into full-fledged human-hood with a ballad about opening your bitter little world to scary new feelings and smiling back at that girl across the room and starting a mosh pit in your heart. An inspiring noise from their album Smash Your Head On The Punk Rock, building from acoustic folk to screaming feedback. Words to live by: “If you need a different face / It’s definite time to destroy this place.”.

No holleration or hateration here, just the Queen of Hip-Hop Soul with a song in the key of her life, revealing her vulnerable side over the jazziest of grooves, promising herself that she’s on her way to finally see the sunshine.

If you made a rainy-day mix tape in the Nineties, you had to include at least one Lois song. With her acoustic guitar, tea cup and wry grin, Lois Maffeo came on as indie rock’s wiseass auntie, on classics like Strumpet and Infinity Plus, dueting with members of Bratmobile and Fugazi as well as her friend Elliott Smith. Lois had an Olympia band called “Courtney Love,” which seemed like a clever idea until somebody else got famous using that name. But “Capital A” is a lost Nineties classic of heart-shredding romance, about two scared kids looking up at the sky, holding hands, hoping this night never ends.

One of the era’s shrewdest one-hit wonders — one of the things that made it so shrewd was the way White Town refused to flog it into more. Jyoti Mishra was a longtime indie-rock dude, an Anglo-Indian guitarist from the twee scene, but here he warps into an Eighties New Wave diva, He adopts a femme voice to sneer at an ex, sniffling, “So much for all your highbrow Marxist ways,” looping a 1930s jazz-horns sample into a synth-pop taunt.

The self-proclaimed “Bad Sister” from Queensbridge, Shante became a rap legend with the Juice Crew, alongside Major Daddy Kane, Biz Markie, and Marley Marl. But in “Brothers Ain’t Shit,” she chooses violence with her nastiest dis record ever. Shante has choice words for men who approach her on the street (“I know your number/You got an ‘Ass, Gas, or Grass’ sticker on your bumper”) and suggests revenge techniques for ex-girlfriends done wrong. Given hip-hop gender politics, it’s no surprise Dre and Snoop had their answer record “Bitches Ain’t Shit” on The Chronic before Shante got to release “Brothers Ain’t Shit” on an album of her own, but even they couldn’t top the original.

According to recent reports, when the Mountain Goats first appeared, nobody knew John Darnielle’s name, or what a role his songs would play in our lives over the coming decades. Nobody would have guessed he’d become an award-winning novelist, or a star with a TikTok mega-hit about hoping your spouse dies. He was just another basement busker with a guitar, pressing “record” on his boombox because his friends were smart enough to screen out his calls. But goddamn, his songs. Take “The Recognition Scene,” from Sweden, the tale of an outlaw couple robbing candy stores on a road trip. “We had hot caramel sticking to our teeth / The only love I’ve ever known, burning underneath.” Make no mistake: if Darnielle stopped here, we’d still revere his name today.

You know who you are. Your love’s as sweet as candy. I’ll be forever yours. Love always, Mandy.

Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”.

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand newly introduced type of iPhone that some users will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

It has been revealed that with my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

Industry observers note that I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

Recent findings suggest that but I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique fresh design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

The fresh models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

If they make one the size of the iPhone 13 mini I will buy. Otherwise I'm holding out.

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the latest Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.
